definition: The difference in electrical potential between two points: the 'push' that drives current. It is always measured between two points, usually a point of interest and ground, in volts (V).
example: "This pin is at 3.3 V" means it is 3.3 V higher than the circuit's ground.

definition: The rate at which electric charge passes a point, written I and measured in amperes. One ampere is one coulomb per second. Sustained conduction current in the basic steady-DC circuit needs a complete return path.
example: A 1 kΩ resistor with 5 V across it carries 5 mA.

definition: How strongly a component opposes electric current, measured in ohms (Ω). Voltage divided by current gives its resistance at an operating point; for an ohmic resistor this ratio stays approximately constant when temperature and other conditions stay fixed.
example: A resistor with 5 V across it and 2.5 mA through it has a resistance of 2 kΩ.

definition: The rate of electrical energy transfer, measured in watts. For a two-terminal part, instantaneous absorbed power is voltage times current when current enters the positive-labelled terminal; for changing signals, average that product to find average power.
example: A resistor with 3.3 V across it and 10 mA through it turns 33 mW into heat.

definition: The electrical power a component turns into heat. Every part has a limit; exceed it and the part overheats, drifts or fails.
example: A 100 Ω resistor across 5 V dissipates 0.25 W, the full rating of a typical small resistor.

definition: The SI unit of electric charge. One ampere of current moves one coulomb of charge past a point every second.
The SI unit of energy. One watt of power is one joule transferred every second.
The current flowing into any junction equals the current flowing out, because charge isn't created or lost. In a single loop this means the same current flows through every part.
example: If 10 mA flows through an LED's series resistor, 10 mA also flows through the LED.

definition: Around any closed loop, the voltage rises add up to the voltage drops. It is how you find the voltage left for one part once the others have taken theirs.
example: With a 5 V supply, 3.3 V across the resistor leaves 1.7 V across the LED.

definition: The conductive metal case or frame of a piece of equipment used as a reference or shield. Whether it is joined to circuit 0 V depends on the design.

The convention that current flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal through the external circuit. Every formula, datasheet and schematic symbol uses it, even though in metal wires the moving charges are electrons drifting the other way.
example: In a forward-biased diode, conventional current flows from anode to cathode.

definition: A negatively charged particle. In metal wires electrons are the charge carriers, so they drift from − to +, opposite to conventional current; both descriptions give the same answers.

A letter in front of a unit that multiplies it by a power of ten: M (mega, 10⁶), k (kilo, 10³), m (milli, 10⁻³), µ (micro, 10⁻⁶), n (nano, 10⁻⁹), p (pico, 10⁻¹²). Case matters: m and M differ by a factor of 10⁹.
example: 100 nF is the same as 0.1 µF.

definition: The international metric system of units, including the volt, ampere, ohm, watt, farad and second, and the metric prefixes used to scale them.
The metric prefix meaning a million (10⁶). Note the capital M; a lower-case m means milli.
The metric prefix meaning a thousand (10³).
The metric prefix meaning one thousandth (10⁻³). Lower-case m; capital M means mega.
The metric prefix meaning one millionth (10⁻⁶), written with the Greek letter µ (mu) or, where that isn't available, a plain u.
The metric prefix meaning one billionth (10⁻⁹).
The metric prefix meaning one trillionth (10⁻¹²).
example: 1000 pF is 1 nF.

definition: One millionth of an ampere. Datasheets often specify input leakage and light-load output figures in microamps.
example: A logic output tested at 20 µA is under a very light load.

definition: One trillionth of a farad (10⁻¹² F). Small ceramic capacitors and stray capacitances are measured in picofarads.
example: The capacitor code 104 means 100,000 pF, which is 100 nF.

definition: A way of writing component values on schematics with the prefix letter (or R for ohms) in place of the decimal point, so a lost dot can't change the value. It is part of IEC 60062.
example: 4k7 means 4.7 kΩ, 2R2 means 2.2 Ω and 100n means 100 nF.

definition: An unbroken current path through a source and load. In the steady low-voltage DC model, breaking the only loop stops sustained conduction current; real circuits may briefly store or transfer charge through capacitance.

A break or very high-resistance path. It stops sustained current in the ideal steady-DC loop, but a voltage may still exist across it. A meter’s OL indication can also mean over-range rather than a literal broken connection.

The path carrying current back to its source to complete a circuit. In ordinary unbalanced audio the sleeve or shield is the signal return; balanced audio uses two signal conductors, with the shield serving a separate screening role.
An adjustable mains-powered DC supply for testing circuits, usually with a voltage setting, a current limit and meters for both.
example: Set the current limit a little above the expected draw before the first power-up.

definition: A supply control that limits delivered current by reducing its output voltage when necessary. It can reduce sustained fault energy, but response time and stored output charge mean it cannot guarantee protection of every component.
example: Select an initial current limit from the actual circuit’s startup needs and weakest component limits, then observe the first power-up.

definition: The brief surge of current a circuit draws when first powered, mostly while its capacitors charge.

A signal carried on one signal conductor and measured against a reference shared by transmitter and receiver. A differential connection instead measures the difference between two signal conductors; balancing also concerns their impedances to the reference.
A connection that passes a signal without a direct electrical path between the two devices' grounds, usually using an opto-isolator or transformer. DIN MIDI is the classic example in a studio.

A diode operating polarity with the anode at a higher voltage than the cathode. Current increases continuously and steeply with voltage; the quoted forward voltage is specified at a test current, not an ideal on/off threshold.
A diode polarity with its cathode at a higher voltage than its anode. It normally carries a small leakage current until reverse breakdown; exceeding its specified reverse limits can damage it.
A way of mounting components with wire leads that pass through holes in a circuit board and are soldered on the other side. Through-hole parts suit breadboards and hand soldering.

Connected end to end, one after another. For components this means one shared current path: the same current flows through each, their voltages add up to the total, and resistances in series add. For filters or processing stages it means the output of one feeds the input of the next.
example: 1 kΩ and 2.2 kΩ in series behave like one 3.2 kΩ resistor.

definition: Components connected across the same two nodes, so their voltages are equal and branch currents add. For two or more ordinary positive finite resistances, the combined resistance is smaller than the smallest branch.
example: Two 10 kΩ resistors in parallel behave like 5 kΩ.

definition: A notation meaning that components share the same two circuit nodes. For two ordinary positive resistors, combine their resistances by dividing their product by their sum.
example: 10 kΩ ∥ 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ.

definition: How easily current flows through something: one divided by its resistance, measured in siemens (S). Conductances in parallel simply add.
example: A 1 kΩ resistor has a conductance of 0.001 S.

definition: A circuit or component drawing current from an output, such as another board, an input or a meter. A passive resistive load from a divider output to ground lowers the effective lower resistance and pulls the voltage down; active or sampling inputs need their own model.
example: A 10 kΩ load on a 10 kΩ/10 kΩ divider from 3.3 V drags it from 1.65 V to 1.1 V.

definition: The resistance a source appears to have in series with its output, helping predict how loading changes its voltage. For a resistive divider fed by an ideal independent voltage source, it is the upper and lower resistors in parallel; source resistance and more complex circuits require additional modelling.
example: A 10 kΩ/10 kΩ divider has an output resistance of 5 kΩ.

definition: A representation of a linear two-terminal network as a voltage source in series with a resistance. For this divider’s independent ideal voltage supply, setting that source to zero makes a short when finding the output resistance. Dependent sources require additional care and cannot simply all be removed.

A circuit that holds an output voltage within a specified tolerance as input and load vary within its operating limits. Dropout, current limit, stability, temperature and capacitor requirements matter; it cannot regulate outside those limits.

A regulator that controls a transistor continuously to hold an output voltage, with excess electrical power usually dissipated as heat. An LDO is a low-dropout type needing comparatively little input-to-output headroom. Noise rejection depends on frequency, headroom, current and the exact design.
The strip of resistive material inside a potentiometer that the wiper slides along. Its end-to-end resistance is the pot's marked value.

A potentiometer taper whose resistance ratio changes nonlinearly with position, often used for analogue volume control. Some audio tapers give about 10% of the unloaded output at mid-rotation, but use the exact manufacturer curve and wiring direction; it need not be an exact mathematical logarithm.

A potentiometer value marking: 10K indicates a nominal 10 kilohm track and the letter denotes a manufacturer-specific taper code. Confirm the code in the datasheet or by an unpowered out-of-circuit measurement.
A component that can't amplify or generate power, such as a resistor, capacitor, inductor or switch.

Coloured bands indicating the nominal value, multiplier and tolerance of a resistor under the relevant marking convention. In the ordinary four-band code, two digits precede multiplier and tolerance; precision five-band parts use three digits.
example: Yellow-violet-red-gold is 4, 7, ×100, ±5%: 4.7 kΩ ±5%.

definition: The international standard that defines the resistor and capacitor colour code and letter-and-digit (RKM) value marking.

The permitted initial departure of a component’s value from its nominal value under specified measurement conditions. A nominal 10 kΩ resistor with five per cent tolerance permits 9.5–10.5 kΩ; temperature and ageing can add other changes.

A preferred-value series containing 24 nominal values in each tenfold range, traditionally associated with 5% tolerance. It includes the E12 values with additional choices between them; the selected part’s datasheet, not the E24 label alone, establishes its tolerance.
A tenfold range, such as 10 to 100 Ω or 100 Hz to 1 kHz. Preferred-value series repeat the same pattern of values in every decade.
A multimeter with a numeric display. Its voltage input is high-impedance, typically around 10 MΩ on DC volts, so it barely loads most circuits.
The insulating material between a capacitor's plates. It sets how much capacitance fits in a given size and how stable it is with voltage and temperature.

Resistance times capacitance, written τ (tau), in seconds. In an ideal first-order RC charging or discharging circuit, each time constant covers about 63.2% of the remaining change, reaching within 1% after about five time constants. Real loading and component behaviour can change that model.
example: A 10 kΩ resistor with a 100 nF capacitor has a time constant of 1 ms.

definition: A curve whose rate of change is proportional to how far it still has to go, so it moves fast at first and then ever more slowly. Capacitors charging through a resistor follow one.

A capacitor using a ceramic dielectric, often built as many thin layers (MLCC). Ordinary ceramic capacitors are non-polarised; their capacitance stability and losses depend on dielectric and construction. A 100 nF ceramic is a common local-decoupling example, but follow the exact device and capacitor specifications.
A non-polarised capacitor with a plastic film dielectric. Stable and low in distortion, so it is used in audio signal paths and filters.

A compact polarised electrolytic capacitor using tantalum. Its stripe usually marks the positive lead, the opposite of aluminium electrolytics; reversed or over-stressed, it can fail short and catch fire.

A component with specified polarity or orientation, such as an LED, diode, polarised electrolytic capacitor or chip. Check the exact part and schematic before powering it; non-polarised parts do not have this restriction.

A larger capacitor, typically an electrolytic of tens to hundreds of microfarads, where power enters a board. It smooths slower, larger load changes; it complements local decoupling but can't replace it.

The maximum voltage a component is specified to withstand under stated operating conditions. Check the highest actual voltage, including ripple and transients, and the exact part’s derating instructions; capacitance, current, temperature and lifetime requirements still matter.
example: For a nominal 5 V rail, establish its maximum peak voltage before choosing the capacitor’s rating.

definition: Deliberately running a part below its maximum ratings, such as voltage, power or temperature, to improve reliability. Manufacturers publish derating guidance.

The change in effective capacitance under a DC voltage. High-permittivity Class 2 ceramic parts can lose a large fraction; the exact part’s curves determine how much, and voltage rating alone does not predict retention.

Ceramic capacitor dielectrics with high capacitance per size but values that shift with temperature, voltage and age. The code describes temperature behaviour: X7R stays within ±15% from −55 to +125 °C.

A stable Class 1 ceramic dielectric with very little temperature dependence and no significant DC-bias capacitance loss. For a comparable package, available capacitance is usually much lower than high-permittivity Class 2 alternatives.
A marking on small capacitors: two digits followed by the number of zeros, in picofarads.
example: 104 means 10 followed by four zeros: 100,000 pF = 100 nF.

definition: A manufacturer of LEDs and displays whose datasheets give typical and maximum forward voltages for each colour.
Datasheet stress limits beyond which a part may be permanently damaged. They are not operating conditions: the part isn't guaranteed to work there, and living near them can shorten its life.
example: The SN74HC00's absolute maximum supply is 7 V, but it is only specified to operate from 2 V to 6 V.

definition: The datasheet table of supply, input and temperature ranges within which a part is guaranteed to meet its specifications. Design inside it, with margin.
example: The SN74HC00 is specified for a 2 V to 6 V supply.

definition: A family of general-purpose 1 A silicon rectifier diodes (1N4001 to 1N4007, differing in reverse-voltage rating), often used for reverse-polarity protection.

A diode designed for rectification, converting alternating current to unidirectional current, or blocking reverse current. A capacitor-input full-wave supply often draws charging pulses twice per mains cycle, contributing a 100 Hz component with UK 50 Hz mains.

A metal–semiconductor junction diode, often with a lower forward drop than an ordinary silicon PN-junction diode at the same current. Exact voltage, leakage, current, reverse-voltage and switching limits depend on the part.
example: The 1N5817 Schottky is specified at 0.45 V maximum at 1 A.

definition: A common 1 A Schottky rectifier diode; its datasheet gives a maximum forward voltage of 0.45 V at 1 A.
A circuit, often just a series diode in the supply line, that stops current flowing if the supply is connected backwards. A simple diode costs its forward drop.

A diode that conducts when a signal exceeds a reference rail by its forward drop, diverting current. Many inputs have such protection, but some do not; the device’s pin-voltage, injection-current and powered-off limits determine safe use.

A diode providing a recirculating current path for a DC relay or motor coil after switch-off. It limits the voltage spike while stored magnetic energy is dissipated; orientation, current, voltage and release-time requirements depend on the drive circuit.

An electrically controlled switch; an electromechanical relay uses a coil to move contacts. A driven DC coil needs a suitable suppression path, such as a correctly oriented flyback diode, chosen with the switching circuit and timing requirements.
Poles are independent circuits controlled together by a switch. Throws are the alternative contacts to which each pole can connect; an extra mechanical off position need not be another throw.
example: A DPDT switch switches two circuits, each between two outputs.

definition: A switch that turns one circuit on and off. Most momentary push buttons are SPST.
A switch with one common terminal that connects to either of two others, so it can route one signal to A or B.
Two SPDT switches moved together by one lever, for example to switch both channels of a stereo signal.
Two on/off switches moved together, switching two separate circuits on and off at once.
A switch that returns to its resting position when released. A normally open momentary button connects while pressed; a normally closed one opens while pressed.

A switch that stays in the selected state after the actuator is released. Latching describes its action, while toggle and push-button describe actuator forms which can be either latching or momentary.

A small momentary push button with a click, common on circuit boards. The usual four-leg type has its legs internally joined in pairs, so check with a continuity test which legs the button actually switches between.
A diagram or table of what each pin of a chip or connector does. Check which side it is drawn from: the view from the front and from the solder side are mirror images.
The dot, notch, bevel, square pad or triangle that identifies pin 1 of a chip or connector. Count the other pins from it.
The common cylindrical audio plug and socket, in 3.5 mm and 6.35 mm (¼ in) sizes. Contacts are named tip, ring and sleeve from the end of the plug.
A jack plug with two contacts: the tip carries the signal and the sleeve is ground and shield. TS connections are unbalanced.
A shape feature that lets a connector fit only the correct way round. Unkeyed headers fit both ways, including the wrong one.
The printed text and outlines on a circuit board, such as reference designators and pin 1 marks.
A group of logic chips built the same way with compatible supply voltages and thresholds, such as 74HC or 74HCT.
Input/output: a pin that connects a chip to the outside world, as an input, an output or either.
A family of processor designs licensed by Arm Ltd and used in many modern 32-bit microcontrollers, including the Cortex-M7 on the Teensy 4.1.
The datasheet threshold for a logic input: V_IH(min) is the lowest voltage guaranteed to be read as a high.
example: TI's SN74HC00 at a 4.5 V supply guarantees a high input from 3.15 V upward within the device's valid input range.

definition: The datasheet threshold for a logic input: V_IL(max) is the highest voltage guaranteed to be read as a low.
example: TI's SN74HCT00 guarantees a low input at or below 0.8 V within the device's valid input range.

definition: The datasheet high-output-voltage guarantee under stated supply, load and temperature conditions. V_OH(min) is the lowest guaranteed high; for TI SN74HC00 at 4.5 V and 4 mA source current, it is 3.98 V at 25 °C and 3.84 V over its commercial temperature range.
example: TI SN74HC00 at a 4.5 V supply guarantees 3.98 V high at 4 mA source current at 25 °C; over the commercial temperature range the limit is lower.

definition: The datasheet guarantee for a logic output: V_OL(max) is the highest voltage it produces for a low, at a stated load current.

The difference between a driver’s worst-case output voltage and the receiver’s guaranteed input threshold, checked separately for high and low. Positive static margins leave that much room for noise and reference offset under the stated conditions; timing and stress limits still need separate checks.
example: A 2.4 V minimum high into a 2.0 V threshold leaves a 0.4 V high margin.

definition: The voltage range between V_IL(max) and V_IH(min), where a logic input's reading is not guaranteed.
A high-speed CMOS logic family. Its input thresholds scale with the supply, so at 4.5 V the SN74HC00 (four NAND gates) only guarantees to read 3.15 V or more as high.

A CMOS logic family with TTL-compatible input thresholds. TI SN74HCT00, with its specified 4.5–5.5 V supply, guarantees high from 2.0 V and low up to 0.8 V. It can accept a lower-voltage driver only when that driver’s guarantees and every other electrical and timing condition match.
The name of a chip's positive supply pin or rail on a datasheet or schematic.
The semiconductor industry standards body that publishes, among other things, standard logic-level definitions such as LVTTL.

Low-voltage transistor-transistor logic, a logic-level convention for 3.3 V systems. Read the exact device’s input thresholds and output guarantees at the stated current and temperature; the label alone does not specify an arbitrary pin’s complete limits.
example: Microchip’s documented 3.3 V LVTTL FPGA I/O setting at 2 mA guarantees a high of at least 2.4 V and a low of at most 0.4 V.

definition: A datasheet figure describing representative behaviour under specified conditions. Unlike a guaranteed limit, it need not apply to every part, so use the stated minimum and maximum guarantees when designing a reliable interface.
The supply voltage, load current, temperature and so on under which a datasheet value is guaranteed. The same parameter can differ greatly under different conditions.
example: For TI SN74HC00 at 4.5 V and 25 °C, the guaranteed high is 4.4 V at 20 µA source current and 3.98 V at 4 mA.

definition: The datasheet section listing guaranteed minimum and maximum values, such as output voltages and input currents, under stated test conditions.
A complete circuit of many transistors on one piece of silicon, in a package with pins. Schematics label them U1, U2 or IC1.
A through-hole chip package with two parallel rows of pins, 2.54 mm apart along each row and 7.62 mm (0.3 in) between rows for narrow types. It straddles a breadboard's centre channel.
A surface-mount chip package with two rows of gull-wing leads, smaller than a DIP.
A sudden spark of static electricity, such as from a person touching a jack. It can reach thousands of volts and damage unprotected inputs.
Current forced into a chip's pin through its clamp diodes when the pin goes beyond a supply rail. Datasheets limit it; the SN74HC00 lists ±20 mA as an absolute maximum.
When a signal driven into an unpowered chip flows through its input clamp diodes into its supply rail and partly powers it. It can cause unintended behaviour or damage.
example: A board’s power LED may glow faintly while its main supply is off if a driven signal feeds its supply rail.

definition: A capacitor placed close to a chip’s supply pin and connected to ground, often a 100 nF ceramic where the device documentation specifies it. It supplies the chip’s fast current pulses through a short path, so the longer supply path’s inductance causes less voltage dip and ringing.
example: TI recommends 0.1 µF at each V_CC pin of the SN74HC00, as close to the pin as possible.

definition: The property of a conductor or coil that opposes changes in current, measured in henries (H). Even a short wire has some, which is why decoupling capacitors must be close to their pins.
The American National Standards Institute. US-style (ANSI/IEEE) schematic symbols draw a resistor as a zigzag; IEC symbols use a rectangle.
The label that identifies each part on a schematic, parts list and board, such as R1, C3 or U2. The letter shows the type: R resistor, C capacitor, D diode, U or IC chip, J or P connector.
A set of pins that are all electrically connected. A schematic is really a list of nets; every pin on a net is at the same voltage, ignoring wire resistance.
example: +3V3, GND and ADC0 are three nets.

definition: A name attached to a wire on a schematic. Every wire with the same label is on the same net, even with no line drawn between them.
A filled dot on a schematic marking where wires connect. Wires that cross without a dot are not connected.
Chip supply pins left off a schematic drawing and connected implicitly. Check the datasheet pinout so they aren't forgotten when wiring.
One group of five holes on a breadboard (a–e or f–j in one row) joined by a spring clip underneath. Everything plugged into a strip is one node.
The gap down the middle of a breadboard separating the a–e and f–j strips. DIP chips straddle it so each pin gets its own strip.

A long strip along the edge of a breadboard, usually marked red (+) and blue or black (−), for distributing a supply. Rails on opposite sides aren't connected, and some boards split each rail halfway.
Unintended capacitance between conductors, such as adjacent breadboard strips. Its value depends on geometry and materials and can affect fast edges, high-frequency signals and high-impedance nodes.
Software, such as git, that records every change to a set of files so you can see history and go back. Keeping wiring notes alongside code keeps them in step.
The common input on a multimeter, where the black lead stays for every measurement.
The multimeter input jack for the red lead when measuring voltage, resistance, continuity and diode test. Move the red lead back here after measuring current.

term: DC volts and AC volts (meter settings)
definition: Multimeter voltage settings: DC volts reads the DC component, while AC volts usually rejects it. Average-responding meters give RMS-calibrated results for sine waves; other waveforms need a suitable true-RMS instrument within its frequency, crest-factor and range limits.

A protective element designed to open a circuit when its specified current-and-time conditions are exceeded. Some meter current inputs are fused and others are not; check the exact manual and replace a fuse only with its specified type and rating.
A meter feature that picks the measurement range automatically. It chooses the scale, not how the meter is connected.

A meter indication that a reading exceeds the selected measurement range. OL can also indicate an open circuit in resistance or diode mode, depending on the instrument; consult its manual before interpreting it.
A small, precise resistor that a meter measures current through by reading the voltage across it. In current mode a meter is nearly a short circuit because of it.

The voltage dropped across a meter’s current-measuring path, including its shunt and fuse or other series resistance. This can change the current being measured; compare the specified burden and lead effects with the circuit’s available voltage and allowed error.
A multimeter setting that beeps when the resistance between the probes is below a low threshold. Use it unpowered to check wires, joints, rails and switches and to find shorts.
A multimeter setting that passes a small current and shows the forward voltage of a diode one way (about 0.5–0.7 V for silicon) and open circuit the other. It often lights an LED faintly.
Oscilloscope scale settings: V/div is how many volts each vertical grid square represents, and time/div how much time each horizontal square represents.
example: At 1 V/div, a 3.3 V logic signal spans just over three squares.

definition: The condition, a voltage level crossed on a rising or falling edge, that starts each sweep at the same point so a repeating waveform stands still on screen.

A passive oscilloscope probe that attenuates the measured voltage by a factor of ten. A matched probe commonly presents about 10 MΩ and less capacitive loading than a comparable ×1 probe, but its impedance and bandwidth depend on the probe and oscilloscope. Set the scope to match the probe’s attenuation.

A probe measuring the voltage difference between two points while tolerating a specified common-mode voltage. Its isolation, grounding, input range and safety ratings depend on the exact probe and instrument; it is not automatically isolated from earth.

A test-instrument measurement category identifying a transient-overvoltage environment, used together with the rated voltage and manufacturer’s instructions. It does not replace training; mains work is outside this low-voltage module.

A resin-based soldering flux that helps remove oxides so solder wets the joint. Rosin is also called colophony; its fume can cause occupational asthma. Use the HSE’s exposure controls, including suitable source capture where required.
A fan and filter or duct that captures soldering fume at the source and removes it, rather than just stirring it around the room.
Tin-lead solder of 63% tin and 37% lead. It is eutectic, melting and solidifying at 183 °C, and flows easily, but contains lead.

An alloy composition with a single melting and solidification temperature, instead of a range containing both liquid and solid. A non-eutectic alloy has a melting range; either joint must remain still during solidification.

Solder made without intentionally added lead; common tin-silver-copper alloys are called SAC. Kester SAC305 melts over 217–219 °C. Temperature, appearance and process requirements depend on alloy, flux and the actual joint.

Restriction of Hazardous Substances rules limit specified substances, including lead, in covered electrical and electronic equipment placed on the relevant market. Scope, exemptions and applicable EU or UK requirements matter; this explains much commercial use of lead-free solder.
A soldering iron that holds its tip at a set temperature. SparkFun suggests 325–375 °C as a starting range for through-hole work.
Coating a soldering iron tip (or a wire) with a thin layer of fresh solder, which protects it and improves heat transfer.
Molten solder flowing out and bonding to a metal surface rather than balling up. A good joint wets both the pad and the lead.
The copper area on a circuit board where a component lead is soldered.
The shape of solder around a joint. A good through-hole fillet is a smooth, concave cone that wets both pad and lead.

A solder joint with poor bonding or disturbed solidification, often associated with insufficient heat, inadequate flux, contamination or movement. Poor wetting, a balled shape and intermittent contact warrant inspection and rework; dullness alone is not proof, especially with lead-free solder.
Unwanted solder joining two adjacent pads or pins, making a short. Remove it with desoldering braid or a clean tip.
A copper pad that has peeled away from the board, usually from too much heat or force.
Fine copper braid coated in flux that soaks up molten solder when heated against a joint.

Two related conductors twisted together, such as a signal and return or a differential pair. Adjacent small loops have opposite orientation, reducing net magnetic pickup when they experience similar fields; cancellation is incomplete with nonuniform fields or imperfect wiring.

An audio device, commonly transformer based, that passes a signal while interrupting a conductive audio-ground path. Check its level, impedance, bandwidth and grounding instructions; never remove a mains protective earth to imitate it.
Noise coupling where two circuits' return currents flow through the same piece of wire or track, so one current's voltage drop appears in the other circuit's reference.
example: 100 mA of LED current through 0.05 Ω of shared ground adds 5 mV to an audio reference.

definition: A low-frequency wiring arrangement giving sub-circuits separate return paths to a common point to reduce shared-impedance coupling. It is not a universal rule for mixed-signal PCB layout, which may require a continuous plane.

Pin labels for the analogue and digital ground connections of a chip such as an audio codec. They identify pin functions, not a universal rule to split grounds; connect them as the manufacturer specifies.

A copper area on a circuit board used as a low-impedance ground reference and return path. Its geometry, breaks, signal routing and frequency affect where return currents flow; follow the board and device layout guidance.
A power supply that switches current on and off rapidly and smooths it, which is efficient but leaves ripple at its switching frequency. Most USB chargers are switch-mode.

Power supply rejection ratio: a measure of how strongly a circuit suppresses effects of supply-voltage changes, often expressed in decibels. Definitions may be input- or output-referred; read the exact datasheet and frequency curve.
A low-noise, low-distortion dual audio op-amp from Texas Instruments whose datasheet includes CMRR and PSRR versus frequency graphs.

A poisonous, colourless, odourless gas associated with incomplete combustion of carbon-containing material. In this module’s electric-soldering example, the identified ventilation hazard is rosin flux fume; do not infer that all heated fumes are harmless.

One million ohms (1 MΩ). A meter or probe with megohm input resistance draws little DC current, but the exact input resistance, capacitance and selected range determine measurement loading. Scope inputs are not universally 10 MΩ.
example: A 1 MΩ load in parallel with 10 kΩ lowers it only to about 9.9 kΩ.

definition: A logic input with thresholds compatible with the specified TTL voltage levels. TI SN74HCT00 accepts high from 2.0 V and low up to 0.8 V at its documented supply; a 3.3 V driver works only if its own output guarantees and all other limits meet those requirements.
example: The SN74HCT00 has TTL-compatible inputs when powered from 4.5–5.5 V.

definition: A low, steady tone tied to the mains supply: 50 Hz in the UK and its harmonics, often with a strong 100 Hz component from rectified power supplies. It is picked up from ground loops, magnetic fields or a poorly filtered supply.
example: 1 mA of loop current in a 0.1 Ω cable shield adds about 100 µV of hum, roughly 70 dB below a −10 dBV signal.

definition: The point in a circuit chosen as the 0 V reference that other voltages are measured against, and usually the return path for current. It need not be connected to the mains safety earth.
example: "This pin is at 3.3 V" means 3.3 V above circuit ground.

definition: The SI unit of conductance: one siemens is the conductance of a one-ohm resistor, so conductance in siemens is one divided by resistance in ohms.
example: A 1 kΩ resistor has a conductance of 0.001 S (1 millisiemens).

definition: The electric charge separated per volt across an ideal capacitor, measured in farads (F). Practical capacitors range from picofarads to thousands of microfarads, with real behaviour and ratings set by the exact part.
example: A 100 nF capacitor with 5 V across it holds 0.5 µC of charge.

definition: Using a diode to conduct when a signal exceeds a reference voltage by its forward drop, limiting the voltage rise if the current has a safe path. Check the signal-source resistance, diode ratings, rail injection and receiving pin limits; it is not automatically normal-operation level conversion.

A small silicon switching diode. For example, the Vishay 1N4148 datasheet specifies a maximum 1 V forward drop at 10 mA; actual drop depends on current and temperature. It is a distinct part number from 1N914 even when applications use them similarly.

Having equal impedances from the two conductors of an audio pair to ground, so interference tends to affect both equally and a differential receiver can reject it. This differs from making a load impedance equal to the source impedance for maximum power transfer.

The continuous current through a voltage divider’s resistor chain while its supply is applied, before any output load is considered. For an ideal unloaded divider it is the supply voltage divided by the sum of the two resistances; it consumes power even when no output current is taken.

A family of digital logic and a related voltage-level convention. In this module TTL concerns electronic input/output levels, not a network or cache time-to-live. Check the exact part’s guaranteed thresholds, output drive, supply and temperature conditions.

The continuous heat a resistor is rated to dissipate under specified ambient temperature, mounting and other thermal conditions. Use the exact part’s derating curve and suitable margin; a wattage label does not promise a cool surface.

A component that stores energy in an electric field by separating charge. An ideal capacitor carries current while its voltage changes and carries no steady DC current once charged; a steady voltage can remain across it. Real parts also have leakage, resistance, inductance and operating limits.

A circuit’s chosen voltage reference and associated return network, often labelled 0 V or GND. Ordinary direct single-ended links need a common voltage reference, while properly isolated interfaces need not join circuit grounds. Ground conductors have impedance, so different points can develop different voltages; protective earth is a distinct safety function.

The voltage across a diode or LED under forward bias at a stated current and temperature. It depends on the exact device and operating conditions rather than being a fixed turn-on threshold; use its datasheet curves and limits when choosing current-limiting or protection parts.
example: Kingbright WP7113ID revision V.14A specifies 1.9 V typical and 2.3 V maximum at 10 mA; these figures are not universal red-LED limits. Checked 16 October 2026.

definition: Preferred-value tables for resistors and capacitors, arranged approximately on a logarithmic scale and repeated in each tenfold range. Actual E12 and E24 values are standard tables, not exact outputs of a geometric formula. Choose a table value appropriate to the required tolerance, then check the resulting circuit; moving to a larger resistance is appropriate for limiting nominal LED current, not every application.
example: The E12 table per decade is 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82. A nominal LED calculation of 325 Ω calls for at least 330 Ω before checking tolerances and voltage variation.

definition: A switch operated by a projecting lever. Toggle describes the actuator, not whether the contacts latch or return when released; check its specified poles, throws and action.
A switch operated by pushing a button. Its contact arrangement and action are separate specifications: it may be momentary or latching, normally open or normally closed.

The SI unit of capacitance: an ideal one-farad capacitor separates one coulomb of charge per volt across it. One microfarad (µF or uF) is one millionth of a farad, and one nanofarad (nF) is one billionth.

A capacitor using an electrochemically formed dielectric layer, often giving a large capacitance for its size. Ordinary polarised types require the marked positive terminal at the higher voltage; specially specified non-polarised types also exist. Observe the exact part’s polarity, voltage, ripple-current, temperature and lifetime limits.

A source of electrical energy for a circuit, with specified voltage and current capability. Its supply voltage is the potential difference between the relevant supply and return terminals; a supply rail is the connection carrying a supply level. Check its output, current-limit and grounding instructions for the actual load.

A resistor placed in the same current path as another component, so the same current passes through both. An appropriately selected value can limit current; its resistance, power rating and the source and load limits still need checking.
example: With assumed drops of 3.3 V at the source and 2.0 V at an LED, a 330 Ω series resistor gives about 3.9 mA nominally.

definition: Constraining the current through an electrical path. A suitably chosen series resistor can limit current for specified source and load conditions; an active power-supply current limit instead reduces output voltage when necessary. Check the exact circuit and ratings, because neither method guarantees protection against every transient or fault.

How a potentiometer’s wiper resistance ratio changes with actuator position. A linear taper changes the ratio roughly in proportion to position; an audio taper uses a different curve suited to volume control. The circuit load can change the resulting output voltage, so taper and loading are separate effects.

The interval allowed for an ADC input to acquire the signal before conversion. In a sampling-capacitor input, the capacitor must settle closely enough to the input voltage during this interval; higher source resistance can require more time. Use the exact ADC model and accuracy requirement.

A specific Kingbright 5 mm red indicator LED. Revision V.14A of its datasheet specifies 1.9 V typical and 2.3 V maximum forward voltage at 10 mA; those test figures do not define a universal red-LED voltage or a recommended drive current. Check the exact device’s ratings and conditions.
